segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if you were raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on the earth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Christ, your life, is revealed, then you too will be revealed with him in glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Put to death, then, the parts of you that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Because of these the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Among them you too once walked, when you were living in these things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now you too must lay them all aside: wrath, rage, malice, slander, foul talk from your mouth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not lie to one another, since you have stripped off the old self with its practices

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created it,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where there is no Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all and in all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: bearing with one another and forgiving each other if anyone has a complaint against someone. Just as the Lord forgave you, so you also must forgive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And over all these put on love, which is the bond of completeness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, the peace to which you were called in one body. And be thankful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, as you teach and admonish one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with gratitude in your hearts to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Husbands, love your wives and do not grow bitter toward them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they do not lose heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Slaves, obey your human masters in everything, not with work done only to be seen, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you serve as slaves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one who does wrong will be paid back for the wrong he did, and there is no favoritism.

notes.note: Most English versions have 'when Christ appears'. The Greek verb means to make visible what was concealed, and it answers 'hidden' in the previous verse: the life now hidden with Christ will be brought into the open when he is. 'Revealed' keeps that connection, and some modern translations render it the same way.

notes.phrase: the parts of you that are on the earth
notes.traditional: your members which are upon the earth
notes.note: The Greek says literally 'the limbs that are on the earth' and then lists vices, as though they were body parts to be killed. The phrase 'on the earth' deliberately repeats verse 2. Many modern versions paraphrase as 'whatever in you is earthly'; the stranger wording here is the Greek's own.

Some important early manuscripts lack these words, and many scholars think they were added by copyists from the parallel at Ephesians 5:6. The SBLGNT prints them as original. 'Sons of' is a Semitic idiom for people characterised by something; here, the disobedient.

The Greek pronoun can be masculine ('among whom', the sons of disobedience) or neuter ('in which', the vices just listed). The first is chosen here because it avoids making the second half of the verse a repetition of the first. If the last phrase of verse 6 is not original, only 'in which' is possible.

notes.traditional: seeing that ye have put off
notes.note: The Greek participles in verses 9 and 10 can give the reason for the command ('since you have stripped off... and have put on') or be commands themselves ('strip off... and put on'). Most interpreters take them as the reason, pointing back to a change that has already happened. The image is of taking off and putting on clothing.

The Greek is literally 'the old human being', traditionally 'the old man'. 'Self' is the usual modern rendering and is used here for clarity. The expression is wider than an individual's personality, though: verse 11 describes the new one as a sphere where ethnic and social divisions no longer hold, and many scholars see a contrast between the old humanity and the new one created in Christ.

'Barbarian' was the Greek term for anyone who did not speak Greek and so stood outside Greek culture. Scythians, peoples from north of the Black Sea, were proverbial in the Greek world as the wildest of barbarians. The pair moves from the outsider to the most extreme outsider.

'Meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a person who is not harsh or self-assertive. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

The phrase is compressed and can be taken more than one way: love is the bond that produces completeness or maturity, or love is the perfect bond that holds the other virtues, or the community, together. The rendering keeps the Greek's own brevity. 'Over all these' continues the clothing image of verse 12, but could also mean 'above all'.

The Greek word can mean 'grace' or 'gratitude'; the surrounding calls to thankfulness in verses 15 and 17 favour the second. The punctuation of the verse is also uncertain. 'In all wisdom' may go with 'dwell' or with 'teach and admonish', and 'with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs' may go with the teaching or with the singing. 'In you' can also be read 'among you'.

The Greek is literally 'masters according to the flesh'. 'Master' here and 'Lord' are the same Greek word throughout verses 22 to 24. The instruction turns on that: slaves have masters on the human level, but their real master is the Lord Christ.
Under Roman law a slave could not normally inherit; inheritance belonged to sons. The promise of an inheritance from the Lord gives slaves the standing of heirs.

notes.phrase: It is the Lord Christ you serve as slaves.
notes.traditional: for ye serve the Lord Christ
notes.note: The verb comes from the same root as 'slaves' in verse 22, which the rendering brings out. Its form can be a statement ('you are serving') or a command ('serve the Lord Christ'). Most translations take it as a statement, as here, though some scholars prefer the command.

candidates.reason: It recurs in vice lists and in the Gospels' divorce sayings, and translators vary between 'fornication', 'sexual immorality', 'prostitution' and 'unchastity'.
English versions vary between 'slave', 'servant' and 'bondservant', and the choice affects both the household codes and the metaphor of believers as slaves of Christ.
The figurative sense of conducting one's life is frequent in Paul and John, and it needs one decision between keeping the Semitic 'walk' and rendering it 'live'.
It occurs across the household codes and in passages about civil authority, where 'submit', 'be subject to' and 'be subordinate' carry different tones for modern readers.
It ranges over 'soul', 'life' and 'self' across the New Testament, and 'soul' often imports a later body–soul dualism, so the senses need governing consistently.
